This page covers 51-2023.00 electromechanical equipment assemblers, who assemble or modify electrically powered mechanical equipment; O*NET14 tasks, RCI, and Zone1–2. Positioning and fastening, wiring, measurement, testing and adjustment, and disassembly and assembly are all included tasks, without equating to electronics engineering design or all repair responsibilities.

entries: Inputs: approved drawings, bills of materials, processes, part identifiers, tolerances, tools, and test requirements.
Tasks: position and align, fasten, wire, measure, inspect and test, and adjust finished products.
Outputs: components conforming to drawings, tolerance records, test records, defects, and handover status.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether versions agree, parts match, and measurements are valid, and when to stop.
Process: check versions and materials, position and assemble, connect and fasten, measure and test, and document and hand over.
Tools: hand and power tools, calipers and micrometers, fixtures, test instruments, drawings, and record forms.
Collaboration: work with process, quality, testing, materials, repair, and safety personnel responsible.
Quality: traceable parts, versions, positions, tolerances, wiring, torque, tests, and anomalies.

Do not alter drawings, bypass protection, remove isolation, or perform unauthorized energized tests on your own. O*NET U.S. education responses show 53% high school; this is a survey rather than a statutory requirement. Check actual training and authorization separately.
Electronics engineers design electronic systems; assemblers produce physical components according to approved drawings.
Engineering technicians support development and testing; assemblers focus on repeatable, controlled assembly and inspection.
Robotics technicians install and maintain automated systems; assemblers do not automatically undertake programming and repair.
Calibration roles ensure measurement values, and repairers diagnose equipment already in use; neither equates to assembling new parts.

career_risk_cards.heading: Risks and control points for electromechanical equipment assemblers

risks.consequence: May cause assembly with incorrect parts and increase rework.
risks.mitigation: Isolate conflicting materials, check approved versions, and refer to process and materials personnel for confirmation.
risks.scenario: Drawing, BOM, or part identifier versions do not agree.

risks.consequence: Measurement conclusions are incomparable, potentially causing incorrect release.
risks.mitigation: Pause judgment, retain original values, and have quality personnel check conditions.
risks.scenario: Measuring instrument status, tolerances, or test conditions are missing.

risks.consequence: May damage components or leave safety problems.
risks.mitigation: Do not release; document anomalies and refer to quality and testing personnel responsible.
risks.scenario: Wiring polarity, fastening, or protection status differs from approved requirements.

risks.consequence: May injure personnel and exceed responsibility.
risks.mitigation: Stop; actually authorized personnel decide under applicable site procedures.
risks.scenario: Unauthorized energized testing, drawing alteration, or protection bypass.

risks.consequence: Subsequent personnel cannot confirm quality status.
risks.mitigation: Add traceable records, refer to process/quality/safety personnel responsible, and retain unresolved items.
risks.scenario: Component, version, measurement, or anomaly records are incomplete.

risks.mitigation: Stop and escalate through the authorization chain.

description.text: Electromechanical equipment assemblers position and fasten parts, wire, measure, test, and document according to approved drawings and specifications. The core goes beyond putting components together: maintain consistent versions, tolerances, wiring, and test conditions, and stop whenever conflicts arise or safety status is unclear.
